beats.narration_text: Research Computing on Explorer and AICR. Logging into Explorer, H P C, with Claude. How to make a key, unlock it once, and let Claude Code log into the Explorer cluster for you, without ever handing it a password.

shot.visual_intent: Film identity and short teaching description, visible immediately; Liam speaks playlist, title, summary

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. First, a correction. To let Claude log into Explorer, you do not hand it your password. You make a key, you unlock it once yourself, and Claude never sees either.

beats.narration_text: Six terms. A private key: a secret file that proves who you are. A public key: its matching half, safe to share. An ssh agent: a helper that holds your unlocked key. BatchMode: a setting that makes ssh refuse to ask any question. A host alias: a short name for the cluster in your ssh config. And a login node: the shared computer you land on when you connect.

beats.narration_text: Explorer lets you in with your Northeastern password. You connect to the login host, answer the first host key question with yes, type the password, and you land on a login node. On our account there was no Duo prompt for ssh. The web portal is different: the documentation says it asks.

beats.narration_text: That works for you at a keyboard. It does not work for Claude. Claude Code runs commands with no keyboard attached, and a password is the one thing you must never hand it. So we replace the password with something the agent can use without ever seeing it. A key.

beats.act: II · Make And Install A Key
beats.narration_text: A key comes in two halves. The private half stays on your computer and proves who you are. The public half is safe to hand out, and Explorer will keep a copy. When you connect, your computer proves it holds the private half that matches.

shot.visual_intent: A kraft key drawn in two halves: the private half (dark outline, a padlock) stays beside the portrait; the public half (lighter, no lock) slides across to the login rack and is filed on a shelf; the two halves briefly line up across the gap with a check.

beats.act: II · Make And Install A Key
beats.narration_text: Make it with ssh keygen. The type is E D twenty-five five-nineteen, a modern default. You choose a passphrase, which locks the private file and which Claude never sees. The command prints where both halves went, and a fingerprint, a short name for this key.

beats.act: II · Make And Install A Key
beats.narration_text: To install the public half, one command: ssh copy id. It asks for your Northeastern password this one time, typed by you, and it reports that one key was added. After this, Explorer knows your key.

beats.narration_text: Now the old problem. Claude cannot type a passphrase. So you unlock the key yourself, once, into a helper called the ssh agent. The agent holds the unlocked key, ssh asks the agent, and the key never passes through Claude.

beats.narration_text: On a Mac, one command: ssh add, with the Apple Keychain flag. You type the passphrase here, in your own terminal. It answers that the identity was added. With the Keychain, the key can reload itself when the agent is emptied.
beats.motion_claim: The real commands and their real output print line by line, each as it is spoken.

beats.narration_text: Then give the cluster a short name. One block in your ssh config. Host explorer. The real host name. Your user name. The key file, and identities only, so ssh offers just this key. Add keys to agent, use keychain, and a keep alive.
beats.motion_claim: The real commands and their real output print line by line, each as it is spoken.

beats.narration_text: Here is a real mistake from this setup, so you do not repeat it. Before that block existed, the test failed: could not resolve host name explorer. Ssh treated explorer as a computer name, because nothing told it otherwise. The fix is the block you just saw.

props.title: Terminal · a real failure, before the config block
lines: ssh: Could not resolve hostname explorer: nodename nor servname provided, or not known

beats.motion_claim: The real commands and their real output print line by line, each as it is spoken.

beats.narration_text: Test it the way Claude will connect. BatchMode makes ssh fail at once instead of asking a question. It printed the user name, and the login node, explorer dash zero one. No password, no passphrase, no Duo.

props.title: IV · Let Claude Do It  ·  your terminal, the BatchMode test

beats.motion_claim: The real commands and their real output print line by line, each as it is spoken.

beats.narration_text: Then Claude Code ran the same login itself, with four read-only commands: who am I, which host, which folder, and my own jobs. The job list printed only its header, because there were none.

props.title: Terminal · Claude Code's own run, read-only
lines: $ ssh -o BatchMode=yes explorer 'whoami; hostname; pwd; squeue -u <explorer-username>'
JOBID PARTITION     NAME     USER ST       TIME  NODES NODELIST(REASON)

beats.motion_claim: The real commands and their real output print line by line, each as it is spoken.

beats.narration_text: From here, Claude follows the rules in the H P C dot M D file. Read only first. Ask before it submits, cancels, or deletes. Never compute on the login node. And if any command ever prompts, it stops and tells you.

shot.visual_intent: The Claude logo chip stands at a login rack; four small rule chips land beside it: 'read-only first' (ticked), 'ask before submit, cancel, delete' (a gate with the portrait holding the key), 'no compute on the login node' (a crossed job box on the login rack), 'prompt: stop and tell you' (a stop mark).

beats.narration_text: Then the hardest test, which is a deliberate one. Empty the agent. It reports no identities. Log in anyway, and it still works, because the Keychain reloaded the key, and the list shows it back. This command empties every key, so our rules say only you run it, on purpose, as a test.

beats.act: V · How It Differs From AICR
beats.narration_text: How is this different from AICR? On Explorer you start with your password, and you make your own key. On AICR there is no password at all: you download a key and a certificate that the AICR certificate authority signed. Your Explorer user name is your university login. Your AICR name is built from it, with an underscore and the institution on the end. And access comes from a project sponsor on Explorer, and from a proposal on AICR.

beats.act: V · How It Differs From AICR
beats.narration_text: What is the same matters more. Both are ssh. Both need you to unlock a key once into the agent. Both are tested with BatchMode. And on both, Claude never holds your password, your passphrase, or your key.

beats.act: V · How It Differs From AICR
beats.narration_text: And what we did not test. Logging in from off campus or another network. The web portal. And whether Research Computing permits automated agent access. The policy pages mention none of them, so ask once, by email to R C help, at Northeastern dot E D U.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Explorer starts with your password, which Claude must never hold. Make a key, install its public half, and keep the private half yours. Unlock the key once into the ssh agent, and give the cluster a host alias. Test with BatchMode, then let Claude run read-only commands. AICR differs: no password, and a key and certificate you download. And on both, Claude never holds your password, passphrase or key.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Log into the Explorer cluster with ssh explorer and run read-only commands only. Run: whoami, hostname, pwd, and s queue for my own user. Tell me the user name, the host, and which folder I land in. Do not submit, cancel or change anything, and do not run computation on the login node. Then check two things yourself. Did Claude run only read-only commands? And did it ever ask for, or print, your passphrase or your key?

props.command: Log into the Explorer cluster with `ssh explorer` and run read-only commands only. Run: whoami, hostname, pwd, squeue -u $USER. Tell me the user name, the host, and which folder I land in. Do not submit, cancel or change anything, and do not run computation on the login node.
output: Check: did Claude run only read-only commands, nothing that submits or changes?
Check: did Claude ever ask for, or print, your passphrase or key? It should not.
